newsitem.title: UK: Physical zinc activity jittery in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Physical zinc activity jittery in Europe.

text.p: Zinc physical business in Europe is nervously backing off as backwardations loom and as industry winds down for the summer, traders said.
"It's a bit of a stand-offish period," one trader said."It's quietening down a little bit due to the vacation season but people are also getting a bit scared of this market."
Three month prices on Thursday hit fresh seven year highs on the London Metal Exchange (LME) of $1,562 per tonne, while tightness in September drove the premium of cash over three months to $37.
Nearby spreads remain in contango, but from September onward backwardations were in force.
A battle is being waged between Chinese smelters which are heavily short and a large European merchant which is long, industry sources and traders said.
"People are standing back, figuring out what the backwardations mean to them," a trader said.

Producers were in a fix since they price their concentrate on the cash price and holders of warrants who had financed at a contango would have to decide whether to pay the backwardation or deliver to the market.
Another trader said business was not bad considering it was summer, but people were waiting until the last minute.

Customers in Europe where economies are recovering still needed to buy after destocking last year and missing out as prices have stubbornly marched higher with barely a correction since January, he added.
Many customers were contracting for physical metal with pricing options that allowed them to agree on the premium at the last minute, another trader said.
"I still have material sitting here unsold with not so much interest," another trader said.

Premiums for special high-grade duty paid zinc in Rotterdam were steady at $50/$55 above LME cash. But more CIS, non-deliverable, material was available and the rates in Rotterdam weakened by about $5 to a $10/$15 discount, traders said.

In general physical premiums in the Far East were under pressure as demand wilts from slow growth and currency devaluations. "There are too few opportunities out there and many people chasing the business," a trader said.
Japan was an exception, where galvanized steel production had seen good gains in the first half of the year, one trader said.
Premiums in the U.S. were also soft, with a U.S. Mint tender scheduled for Tuesday. Premiums were expected to ease to 3.55 to 4.75 cents a lb over LME cash from 4.25 to 4.75 cents previously.
A European trader said his U.S. customers had already done a lot of buying. "In general they saw the business was very strong and bought and priced forward."
